project.name: Open Psychology Interactives — Simplified Edition
project.description: Shorter, single-purpose versions of the 75 Open Psychology Interactives. Each keeps the mechanism of the activity it pairs with and reduces the lesson around it to one teaching job, at roughly 3 to 7 minutes rather than 15 to 30.

modules.summary: Attention, memory and judgement: what the system does with limited capacity, and what that costs.

activities.title: Posner Spatial Cueing
activities.summary: A spatial-cueing experiment the learner runs on themselves. A box brightens, then a target appears, sometimes where the cue pointed and sometimes not. Their own reaction times separate the benefit of a valid cue from the cost of an invalid one, against their own neutral baseline.
activities.teachingJob: moving attention without moving the eyes, and why a cueing effect is two effects rather than one

activities.title: Visual Search Laboratory
activities.summary: Find a target defined by one feature, then one defined by two features in combination, at eight, sixteen and thirty-two items. The learner's own reaction times are fitted to produce two search functions, and the number that matters is the slope rather than the speed.
activities.teachingJob: why the slope of a search function matters more than how fast anyone was

activities.title: Inattentional Blindness
activities.summary: A demanding count on a dense static display that also contains an object nobody mentioned, followed by a recognition question and the same display again with everything marked. The demonstration works once, and the page is built so that nothing before the task gives it away.
activities.teachingJob: attention, awareness, and an object in plain view that goes unreported

activities.title: Change Blindness
activities.summary: A street scene alternates with itself, with a blank quarter-second in between, and one large thing keeps changing. Most people cannot find it. The same task with the blank removed, on a fresh scene, takes a moment.
activities.teachingJob: why a quarter-second of blank makes a large obvious change nearly impossible to find

activities.title: Attentional Blink
activities.summary: Letters arrive ten a second. Somewhere in each stream is a digit, and somewhere after it there may be an X. Reporting the digit costs a few hundred milliseconds in which the X is displayed, looked at, and not seen, and the learner's own accuracies draw that curve.
activities.teachingJob: the few hundred milliseconds after finding one target in which a second one is not seen

activities.title: Stroop Interference Laboratory
activities.summary: Six untimed practice trials, then 45 scored trials naming the ink colour of congruent, neutral and incongruent words. Results are withheld until the block ends, and the learner's own reaction times are then split into two effects measured from the neutral baseline: the cost of a conflicting word and the benefit of a matching one.
activities.teachingJob: colour-word interference, and why a neutral baseline turns one effect into two

activities.title: What Got Through
activities.summary: Two streams of words arrive side by side. The learner has a job to do with one of them and is told to ignore the other entirely, then answers two questions about the ignored stream: whether it changed, and what it was about. The two answers usually come apart.
activities.teachingJob: what survives from a stream you are ignoring, and what the selection theories were built to explain

activities.title: Dual-Task Capacity Laboratory
activities.summary: Two trivial speeded tasks are performed alone and then together. Both slow down, and the cost for each is measured against the learner's own single-task speed rather than against anyone else's.
activities.teachingJob: what doing two easy things at once actually costs, measured against your own baseline

activities.title: Working-Memory Load Laboratory
activities.summary: Hold two letters or six in mind, do four paced judgements about something else, then pick the letters out of a grid. The cost of the extra load depends on whether the in-between task is made of the same material as the letters.
activities.teachingJob: why what you are doing in between matters as much as how much you are holding

activities.title: Remembering a Word Nobody Said
activities.summary: Two lists are read by two named people, each built so that every word points at one word that never appears. At test the learner judges ten words three ways, and the words they are surest about include one that was never on the screen.
activities.teachingJob: how a word that was never presented gets remembered confidently, and attributed to someone

activities.title: Decision Framing Laboratory
activities.summary: Four decisions about resources at risk, made one at a time with nothing explained. Two pairs of them turn out to contain identical numbers, described once in terms of what is saved and once in terms of what is lost.
activities.teachingJob: how the same outcomes described two ways produce opposite choices

activities.title: Two Things Called Attention
activities.summary: Resolve an ambiguous pronoun yourself, then work out by hand the weights a language model would produce over the same sentence, then sort five claims by whether they apply to what you did, to what the model does, to both, or to neither.
activities.teachingJob: what the operation called attention actually computes, and why sharing a name is not sharing a mechanism

modules.summary: Sampling, estimation, error and power: the reasoning behind a result rather than the arithmetic of one.

activities.title: Research Question to Method Mapper
activities.summary: Three fictional research questions, read twice each: what kind of answer the wording asks for, and what kind of study could produce it. There is no answer key, options carry three standings rather than two, and the third question is deliberately unsettled.
activities.teachingJob: reading a research question for what would count as an answer

activities.title: Operationalisation Laboratory
activities.summary: Build a measurement plan for academic engagement from four candidate measures and watch two consequences move at once: how much of the construct the plan reaches, facet by facet, and how much of what it records is not the construct at all. Adding measures to close one gap widens the other.
activities.teachingJob: operationalisation, construct coverage and the trade-off between under-representation and irrelevant variance

activities.title: Confound Detective
activities.summary: One fictional study with a confident causal claim, in two phases: sort four variables into confound, nuisance, part of the treatment and constant, then repair the design and watch the reported estimate walk toward a true effect the study cannot see. One repair removes no bias at all.
activities.teachingJob: confounding, and why bias and noise are different problems with different fixes

activities.title: Sampling Bias Simulator
activities.summary: A generated population of 4,000 fictional students whose true mean is known, three recruitment methods and repeated draws. The teaching target is the difference between an estimate that scatters and an estimate that is systematically off.
activities.teachingJob: sampling bias, sampling variability, and which one a larger sample fixes

activities.title: Thematic Analysis Coding Laboratory
activities.summary: One invented interview extract. The learner writes a code of their own, then sets it beside three defensible coding passes over the same words. Nothing is marked, no agreement is computed, and the page says why agreement is not the criterion for this method.
activities.teachingJob: coding as an analytic act, and why competent analysts differ

activities.title: Theme or Topic?
activities.summary: One cluster of coded extracts and four candidate statements about it, sorted one at a time into a topic summary, a staging post, a developed theme, or something the data cannot carry.
activities.teachingJob: topics, staging posts, themes and overreach in qualitative analysis

activities.title: Reflexivity and Alternative Themes
activities.summary: The same six invented extracts, two research questions and two theoretical lenses, giving four prepared accounts. Two pairings are coherent and two pull against themselves, and the mismatch is visible from outside.
activities.teachingJob: reflexivity, and why the account follows from the question and the lens

activities.title: Sampling Distribution and p-Value Simulator
activities.summary: Two groups drawn from the same population, so the true difference is exactly zero. Repeating that builds the sampling distribution, an observed difference is marked on it, and the p-value is shown both as an area under the reference normal and as a count of simulated studies.
activities.teachingJob: p-values as tail areas, and what they are not

activities.title: Confidence Interval Laboratory
activities.summary: A simulated population with a true mean of exactly 12. Each study draws its own sample and reports its own interval, the intervals stack up against the fixed truth, and only one of the three controls changes how often they contain it.
activities.teachingJob: what the ninety-five per cent in a confidence interval refers to

activities.title: ANOVA F-Ratio Visualiser
activities.summary: Three groups are drawn from normal populations whose separation, spread and size the learner controls, and a real one-way ANOVA is computed on the generated sample. Separation raises F, within-group spread lowers it, and sample size raises it without the populations changing at all.
activities.teachingJob: what the F ratio is actually a ratio of, and the three separate things that move it

activities.title: Factorial Interaction Detective
activities.summary: A 2 by 2 design with four cell means the learner edits directly. Both main effects and the interaction update as arithmetic on those four numbers, and two further controls show how much of an apparent interaction is the axis it was drawn on and how much survives the uncertainty in the means.
activities.teachingJob: what an interaction is, and how much of the one you can see is the axis rather than the data

activities.title: What a Covariate Can and Cannot Buy
activities.summary: A fictional reading programme with a September score as covariate. A real ANCOVA runs on the generated cohort, showing the unadjusted difference, the adjusted difference and the precision each buys. Switching the design between random allocation and two intact classes changes no arithmetic at all, and changes the conclusion completely.
activities.teachingJob: what adjusting for a covariate does to an estimate, and why only the design decides what the estimate means

activities.title: The Same Mark, Two Different Distributions
activities.summary: A normal curve whose mean and spread the learner controls, drawn on a score axis that never moves, with the same axis relabelled in standard deviations directly beneath it. A mark stays where it is while the distribution slides underneath, and its z-score, percentile and tail areas change completely.
activities.teachingJob: why a raw score means nothing on its own, and what standardising actually does to the axis

activities.title: Central Limit Theorem Simulator
activities.summary: Two panels on one shared value axis: a population that is nothing like normal, with the most recent sample marked beneath it, and a histogram of the mean of every sample drawn so far. Only the lower panel changes shape, and the theory sits beside the simulation while it does.
activities.teachingJob: sampling distributions, the central limit theorem and what it does not claim about data

activities.title: How Much Do Two Groups Overlap?
activities.summary: Guess how much of the lower group still beats the average of the higher group at a large effect, then see it. Two normal curves with their overlap shaded, and Cohen's d, the overlap, the probability of superiority and U3 all describing the same picture.
activities.teachingJob: how much two distributions still overlap at a large effect, and why an effect size says nothing about whether an effect is real

activities.title: The Same Finding, Twice
activities.summary: An independent-samples t-test read off one figure: the distribution of t when the two populations are identical, with the observed statistic marked and the two-tailed area shaded. Adding people moves t and p a long way and leaves Cohen's d exactly where it was.
activities.teachingJob: what a t-test actually asks, and why the sample size changes the answer without changing the finding

activities.title: What Gets Published From a Small Study
activities.summary: Two thousand honest studies of an effect that is genuinely there. Every estimate is kept, the significant ones are marked, and the distribution as a whole lands on the truth while the significant subset overstates it, sometimes enormously and occasionally in the wrong direction.
activities.teachingJob: why the significant results from small studies overstate effects even when everyone is honest

activities.title: What r Cannot See
activities.summary: Twenty-four fixed observations and one the learner can move anywhere. Two fitted lines are drawn, through all twenty-five points and through the other twenty-four, so a single point's influence is visible as a gap rather than only as a change in a number.
activities.teachingJob: what a correlation coefficient measures, what it cannot see, and how much one observation can move it

activities.title: Why It Is Called Least Squares
activities.summary: Twelve observations and a line set by hand with two sliders. Every residual gets a real square whose area is the residual squared, so the quantity being minimised is drawn rather than described, and the exact least-squares solution is revealed only after the learner has tried.
activities.teachingJob: what least squares actually minimises, drawn as the squares it is named after

activities.title: Does the Spread Stay the Same?
activities.summary: A regression line through sixty people, and one question: does the scatter around it stay about the same width across the range? The line is then taken out, leaving only the misses, and three groups that produce almost the same slope turn out to look completely different once it is.
activities.teachingJob: whether the spread around a regression line stays the same across the range, and why the residual plot is the only way to see it

activities.title: The Garden of Forking Paths
activities.summary: One fictional dataset of 90 students generated with no group difference on anything, and four defensible analysis choices over it giving 72 complete reportable analyses. The learner walks a few paths, gets a real p-value from each, and then sees every path they did not take.
activities.teachingJob: researcher degrees of freedom, and what choosing an analysis after seeing the data does to a p-value

modules.summary: Paradigms run first and read about second, plus the logic that turns a pattern of deficits into a claim.

activities.title: Double Dissociation Detective
activities.summary: Four fictional case files, each score read against its own control group. A single dissociation leaves the rival explanation standing, a second person with the same pattern leaves it standing too, and only a reversal rules it out. A test-length control then shows that the same four percentages can be a double dissociation or no evidence at all.
activities.teachingJob: dissociation logic, control-referenced inference and what measurement precision entitles you to claim

activities.title: How Sure Can One Case Make You?
activities.summary: One fictional case, one localisation claim, and the learner's own confidence in it rated before each of three complications arrives. Their line is drawn against a ceiling that only ever falls.
activities.teachingJob: why a single lesion case supports much less localisation inference than it feels like

activities.title: Network Disconnection Mapper
activities.summary: Three regions joined by three pathways, and three tasks that each need two regions and the pathway between them. Damaging a region takes out the tasks that share it; cutting a pathway takes out one task with both its regions intact.
activities.teachingJob: how a deficit can come from a cut connection rather than from damage to any region

activities.title: Neglect or Blindness?
activities.summary: Three fictional profiles, a comparison and two patients, run line bisection and star cancellation. Both patients miss things on the left, and only cancellation separates neglect from a loss of the left visual field.
activities.teachingJob: telling neglect from field loss, and why the obvious task is the wrong one

activities.title: Where the Cut Is
activities.summary: Break the visual pathway at one of five points and watch which parts of which eye's field go dark. Two of the sites produce the identical pattern, which is the point at which the forward exercise stops being a lookup table.
activities.teachingJob: how the shape of a field defect locates the damage that caused it

activities.title: What Each Profile Can Decide
activities.summary: Two claims about memory and three fictional profiles, judged in every combination. One profile has both abilities impaired and is included precisely because it decides nothing.
activities.teachingJob: which claims a case can settle, and which it cannot settle however severe it is

activities.title: Which Measure Separates Them?
activities.summary: Four fictional language profiles across four measures. The learner predicts which single measure will most separate a given pair, and the three pairings offered end on the case where the separating measure is neither profile's worst score.
activities.teachingJob: why the useful measure is the one the two candidates differ on, not the one either scores lowest on

activities.title: What One Score Hides
activities.summary: Four capacities feed three executive tasks with different weights, and the three task scores are averaged into one composite. A search finds a different capacity profile with the identical composite, which is the whole argument.
activities.teachingJob: why a single executive score cannot say what is wrong, and what the pattern across tasks adds

activities.title: Building a Split-Brain Trial
activities.summary: Choose which side of fixation a word appears, how the person is asked to answer, whether the corpus callosum is intact, and how long the word is up. The classic result requires a particular value of all four, and lengthening the exposure alone abolishes it.
activities.teachingJob: the four conditions the classic split-brain result needs, and what happens when one is removed

activities.title: Where Recognition Breaks
activities.summary: A five-step model of recognising a person, with expression branching off early. Impairing any one step produces a distinct profile of which questions can still be answered, and all five profiles differ.
activities.teachingJob: why recognising a face, knowing who someone is, and producing their name can fail separately

activities.title: What Your Battery Cannot Say
activities.summary: One fictional referral, eight questions it raises, ten tasks and eighty minutes. Full coverage needs ninety, so every battery leaves something open, and the report says what.
activities.teachingJob: why the useful half of an assessment report is the list of what was not assessed

activities.title: What Is the Score Actually Made Of?
activities.summary: A fictional patient's score on a practised task climbs over two years. Four contributions with different time courses are stacked underneath it, and a task they never practised rises only by the restitution band, so the gap is everything that did not generalise.
activities.teachingJob: what a rising recovery score is actually made of, and how much of it generalises

modules.summary: Influence, categories and power, and the question of where a finding ends and an interpretation of it begins.

activities.title: The Method Comes Last
activities.summary: One fictional school and three starting points. Declare what you take disruption to be, make two decisions, and watch a study assemble itself that can answer one question and not the others.
activities.teachingJob: why the decision that shapes a study most is the one taken before it starts

activities.title: Where the Prevalence Comes From
activities.summary: Five people describe something difficult. A line drawn across four hundred others gives the condition a prevalence, and a three-item questionnaire gives it a membership. Neither number was discovered, and no three items find all five people.
activities.teachingJob: how a description acquires a prevalence and a membership, neither of which was found

activities.title: Four People, One Score
activities.summary: Four fictional colleagues with identical attitude scores speak up in 25, 8, 4 and 14 of thirty meetings, and across three hundred people the attitude-behaviour correlation more than doubles when everybody is put in the same kind of room.
activities.teachingJob: why the same attitude produces completely different behaviour, and what that does to a correlation

activities.title: Two Reasons to Agree
activities.summary: Six fictional conditions on one task. Taking the audience away removes about twenty-one points of agreement when the display is easy and about eleven when it is ambiguous, because a different route is doing the work.
activities.teachingJob: how to tell normative from informational influence, and why a conformity rate needs a room

activities.title: Nine Things She Said
activities.summary: Five frameworks for the self applied to the same nine statements. Each makes exactly two central and has no concept at all for at least two, and one statement is central to none of them.
activities.teachingJob: why every framework for the self has something it cannot see

activities.title: Five Ways to Write It Up
activities.summary: Eight undisputed events and five accurate accounts of them. Each produces a different kind of person, makes a different next step obvious, entitles somebody different to speak, and four of the five have nowhere to put the decision that started it.
activities.teachingJob: how an accurate account decides what kind of person somebody is and what happens next

activities.title: The Frame You Take With You
activities.summary: Eight trials watching a point of light drift in a dark field, judged on a 1 to 10 scale: three alone, three with three simulated others generated from your own opening judgements, and two alone again once they have gone. Whatever you do, the chart is yours and neither outcome is the right one.
activities.teachingJob: why a figure worked out with other people is still there when they have gone

activities.title: Ahead, or Better Off
activities.summary: Four allocations between two anonymous strangers when you cannot allocate to yourself. The option that puts your category furthest ahead gives it fewer points than the option that gives it most, on all four.
activities.teachingJob: why people pay points to be further ahead when they cannot benefit at all

activities.title: How Many, and At What
activities.summary: Four fictional afternoons and one toggle. Two of them score identically on the measure an account of lost restraint tracks, and their concentration figures are 0.12 and 0.76.
activities.teachingJob: why two theories of crowd action disagree about shape rather than about amount

activities.title: Power Lens Laboratory
activities.summary: One fictional institutional case and three analyses of power applied to the same five items, in the same order, every round. Each lens makes a different item the strongest evidence, leaves a different part of the file in shadow, and implies a different thing to go and change - and no single remedy reaches the other two mechanisms.
activities.teachingJob: power, critical analysis and the consequences of a theoretical lens for intervention

activities.title: What the Instrument Actually Sees
activities.summary: Four instruments all published as measurements of prejudice. Each directly observes something much narrower, and the fourth is not a measure of individuals at all.
activities.teachingJob: what a measure of prejudice records, and how far that is from what it is called

activities.title: Where the File Stops
activities.summary: Four measurements of individuals support an explanation in terms of individuals. Then the rota, the queue, the target and a comparison team arrive, and nothing from the first round has been withdrawn.
activities.teachingJob: why what somebody measured decides what the explanation can be about

modules.summary: Traits, structure and measurement: what a score supports, and what it cannot be asked to carry.

activities.title: How Much Room Does the Situation Leave?
activities.summary: Four fictional people observed in two settings, with one slider for how much the setting dictates behaviour. Raising it squeezes the people together without changing them, and the two settings never agree about who does most.
activities.teachingJob: why the same people look alike in one setting and quite different in another

activities.title: One Moment, or the Whole Fortnight?
activities.summary: Two fictional people, sampled four times a day for a fortnight. Judge them from one reading each, then average more moments and watch a twenty-point difference fall to nothing while a difference in variability stays exactly where it was.
activities.teachingJob: why one observation cannot tell you what somebody is generally like

activities.title: Turn the Axes, Change Every Number
activities.summary: Twelve markers sit fixed in the plane of a two-factor solution. Rotate the axes and every loading changes while the fit, each communality and the total variance stay exactly where they were.
activities.teachingJob: what rotation changes in a factor analysis, and what it cannot change

activities.title: Same Score, Different People
activities.summary: Two fictional people score identically on a broad trait and behave differently. See what the average covered up, then change what the questionnaire asks about and watch the two unchanged people swap places.
activities.teachingJob: what a broad trait score averages away, and why the tie depended on the questionnaire

activities.title: Chasing Alpha
activities.summary: A ten-item scale where you choose how many items are near-duplicates of one another. Alpha climbs past 0.94, the content narrows from five areas to one, and the correlation with the outcome falls by about a quarter.
activities.teachingJob: why a high Cronbach's alpha is not evidence that a scale is any good

activities.title: Reverse-Item Disaster
activities.summary: A six-item fictional scale with two reverse-keyed items that nobody recoded. The learner repairs each reverse item in turn and watches Cronbach's alpha and every item-total correlation move: alpha barely shifts after the first repair, because the second item is still pulling the other way, and only both together give a scale that behaves.
activities.teachingJob: reverse keying, and what an unrecoded item does to a scale's reliability statistics

activities.title: Four Ways to Answer the Same Questionnaire
activities.summary: Four fictional respondents with identical true standing use a five-point scale differently. Reverse-worded items rescue one of them almost exactly and do nothing whatever for the other two.
activities.teachingJob: what reverse-worded items fix, and what they leave exactly as they were

activities.title: The Same Difference, Twice Over
activities.summary: Two groups differ by 0.20 on a four-item scale. One slider moves that difference between being entirely one item behaving differently and entirely a real difference in the trait, without the observed means changing at all.
activities.teachingJob: why a group difference in scores is not yet a group difference in the trait

activities.title: Five Explanations, All of Them Fit
activities.summary: Five accounts of why one fictional person volunteered, all of which fit. Request the evidence, watch two fall, and notice that one of the survivors survived by never committing itself to anything.
activities.teachingJob: why an explanation that fits everything has told you nothing

activities.title: No Best Battery
activities.summary: Sixty minutes of testing time and seven generic task families. Build a battery, then change what the assessment is for and watch a good battery become a poor one with no task changing.
activities.teachingJob: why a test battery cannot be good or bad until you say what it is for
topics: validity as a property of a use

activities.title: A General Factor With No General Ability
activities.summary: Six tests, fifteen hundred small independent processes, and no general ability anywhere in the model. Every correlation comes out positive and a single general factor reproduces the whole matrix to within a couple of hundredths.
activities.teachingJob: why every cognitive test correlating with every other proves less than it seems

activities.title: Take the Words Out and See What Is Left
activities.summary: Design a reasoning task from four decisions and watch what each one demands beyond reasoning. Taking every word out removes the reading demand and raises two others.
activities.teachingJob: why a test with no words in it still assumes a great deal

activities.title: Equally Accurate, or Equally Fast
activities.summary: Two fictional people on the same task, one better at it at every speed. Move one dial and they look identical on accuracy, move it again and they look identical on time.
activities.teachingJob: why a score and a reaction time have to be read together or not at all

activities.title: The Same Genes, A Different Heritability
activities.summary: One fictional population, one slider for how much people's circumstances differ, and a genetic variance that never moves. Heritability runs from 0.19 to 0.67 without a single gene changing.
activities.teachingJob: why heritability is a fact about a population and not about a person

activities.title: Three Findings, Two Lines
activities.summary: Two straight lines that never move, and a window that does. Sampled at the adverse end they show a vulnerability, at the supportive end an advantage, and across the middle both at once.
activities.teachingJob: why the same interaction supports three different theories depending on where you looked

activities.title: It Correlates. So What?
activities.summary: A fictional new questionnaire correlates around 0.4 with the outcome at every setting of one control, while what it adds beyond the measures already available falls from ten percentage points of explained variance to almost nothing.
activities.teachingJob: why a measure correlating with an outcome does not mean it is worth having

activities.title: Same Average, Six Very Different Weeks
activities.summary: Three fictional people with identical average self-esteem and identical-looking weeks. Deliver one setback and how much they move, what moves them and how long it lasts come apart.
activities.teachingJob: the four things a single self-esteem score collapses into one

activities.title: Where the Line Goes
activities.summary: Four invented profiles on two dimensions, a line you can move and two rules that can draw it. Two profiles change sides when the rule changes, and neither of them moves.
activities.teachingJob: what changes when a continuum is cut into a category, and who decides
